Strategist picks keywords from a monthly list. A freelance writer is assigned and drafts independently with no brief beyond the keyword. Drafts come back and go straight to the CMS, reviewed only if something looks obviously wrong.

placeholders.name: ROLES + REALISTIC OUTPUT, e.g. "1 strategist, 2 writers (partly AI-assisted), 1 editor, realistic capacity 6-8 pieces/week"
placeholders.what: Your team's actual roles and how much content they can genuinely produce per week — an honest capacity number, not an aspirational one. This is what keeps the resulting pipeline something your real team can run rather than a diagram sized for a team you don't have.
examples: 1 strategist, 2 writers (partly AI-assisted), 1 editor, realistic capacity 6-8 pieces/week
1 person doing everything part-time, realistic capacity 2 pieces/week
2 in-house writers, 3 freelancers, 1 editor, 1 SEO specialist, realistic capacity 15 pieces/week

placeholders.name: e.g. "comparison pages and how-to guides"
placeholders.what: The main type or types of content this pipeline needs to handle — different content types (comparison pages, how-to guides, news/trend pieces, product pages) sometimes need different quality gates, so naming the type keeps the pipeline relevant.
examples: Comparison pages and how-to guides
Local service landing pages
Long-form buyer's guides and shorter blog posts

variations.label: Lightweight version for a one- or two-person team
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a very small team (a solo operator or a two-person team) where a multi-stage formal pipeline with named roles at each gate would be unrealistic overhead.
variations.prompt:
Help me design a lightweight SEO content process with real quality checks for a very small team — do not assume separate people for each stage, since the same one or two people do everything.

Our current process: [DESCRIBE STAGES AS THEY ACTUALLY HAPPEN]
Team and capacity: [ROLES + REALISTIC OUTPUT]
Target content types: [CONTENT TYPES]

Give me 3-4 stages maximum, each with one simple, checkable pass/fail criterion the same person can self-apply before moving to the next stage (e.g. a personal checklist), and the single most likely place quality slips when one person is doing everything.

variations.label: Version emphasizing AI-content risk specifically
variations.whenToUse: Use this when a large share of the draft is AI-generated and you're specifically worried about factual errors or generic content making it to publish, more than about workflow bottlenecks.
variations.prompt:
Help me design an SEO content pipeline with quality gates specifically focused on catching problems unique to AI-assisted drafting — invented statistics, generic content that doesn't serve search intent, and factual errors — in addition to the standard editorial gates.

Our current process: [DESCRIBE STAGES AS THEY ACTUALLY HAPPEN]
Team and capacity: [ROLES + REALISTIC OUTPUT]
Target content types: [CONTENT TYPES]
Share of the draft that's AI-assisted: [e.g. "first draft is 80% AI-generated, human edited"]

For the fact-check and SEO/intent stages specifically, give me concrete pass/fail criteria aimed at AI-specific failure modes (e.g. "every statistic has a live source checked within 30 days" or "the draft directly answers the target search intent within the first 3 sentences, confirmed by a human reader, not just present somewhere in the piece").

variations.label: Version for scaling up an already-working pipeline
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you already have a working pipeline at a smaller volume and need to redesign it for higher output without losing the quality gates that are currently working.
variations.prompt:
We already have a working content pipeline at a smaller volume and want to scale output without losing quality. Here's our current pipeline and what's actually working well about it — don't change what's working, focus on where it would break at higher volume.

Current pipeline and what's working: [DESCRIBE STAGES AS THEY ACTUALLY HAPPEN, noting which gates are currently effective]
Current capacity vs. target capacity: [e.g. "currently 6 pieces/week, need to get to 15/week"]
Team: [ROLES]

Tell me specifically which stage will become the bottleneck first as volume increases, whether that stage needs more AI assistance, a process change, or more headcount, and how to adjust the quality gate at that stage so it still catches real problems at the higher volume.

followUps.label: A quality gate is too vague — make it checkable
followUps.prompt: The quality gate for the "[STAGE NAME]" stage is still too vague to actually check against. Rewrite it as a specific, concrete criterion someone could verify yes/no, not a general statement about quality.

followUps.label: AI-vs-human split doesn't match our real risk tolerance
followUps.prompt: I think [STAGE NAME] needs more human review than you assigned it, given how much it affects our clients directly. Revise the AI-vs-human split for that stage specifically and explain the tradeoff.

followUps.label: Push harder on the failure point
followUps.prompt: Go deeper on the failure point you identified — walk me through exactly what it would look like in practice if this pipeline broke down there, and give me one leading indicator I could watch for that would tell me it's starting to happen before it causes a real problem.

followUps.label: Turn this into a one-page reference doc
followUps.prompt: Condense this whole pipeline into a one-page reference document I could pin for the team — just the stage names, the pass/fail criterion for each, and who owns each stage. Cut all the explanatory reasoning.

seo-a1-seo-content-production-pipeline-q.walkthrough:
Priya leads content strategy at a small SEO agency and has watched their AI-assisted content output nearly triple in the last six months — but so has the number of pieces going out with a thin fact-check or an off-intent angle that a client later flagged. She wants a real pipeline instead of the current informal habit of "writer drafts with AI help, editor skims before publishing."

She opens ChatGPT and describes her current process honestly, including that fact-checking mostly doesn't happen unless the editor happens to catch something. She lists her real team — one strategist, two writers who are partly AI-assisted, one editor working part-time — and states their realistic capacity as six pieces a week, not the eight they've been aspirationally aiming for. Target content types: comparison pages and how-to guides.

The response returns a six-stage pipeline from brief through editorial sign-off, sized to her actual team. Each stage has a concrete gate: the fact-check gate requires every statistic and named tool feature to have a live source checked within the last 30 days, with unchecked claims removed before moving forward; the SEO/intent gate requires the draft to answer the core search intent within the first three sentences, confirmed by a second reader, not merely present somewhere in the piece. AI assistance is marked for the outline and first-draft stages; humans are required for fact-checking and final sign-off. The flagged failure point: their part-time editor is the likely bottleneck at six pieces a week.

Priya sends the follow-up asking ChatGPT to condense the whole thing into a one-page reference doc she can pin in their shared workspace. She pilots it on three real pieces before rolling it out fully. Building the pipeline took about twenty-five minutes; catching what would have been an unverified statistic on the very first piloted piece took about two.
